questions.q: State the three core features that define caste as a system of stratification according to the NCERT textbook.
questions.a: The three core features are: (1) hierarchy based on purity-pollution, (2) hereditary occupation, and (3) endogamy (marriage within the caste). A wrong answer that lists “untouchability” or “varna” instead reveals the student is confusing specific practices or the four-fold varna model with the structural pillars of the jati-based caste system.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why endogamy is considered the “key” to maintaining the caste system, using the concepts of hierarchy and hereditary occupation.
questions.a: Endogamy prevents mixing of castes, which would blur the purity-pollution hierarchy and break the link between birth and occupation. If people married across castes, children would have mixed ritual status, undermining the hereditary claim to a specific occupation and rank. A wrong answer that says “endogamy preserves culture” misses the structural point: it preserves the *stratification system* by closing the boundaries that hierarchy and hereditary occupation depend on.

questions.q: A village has three castes: Brahmins (priests), Kumhars (potters), and Chamars (leather workers). The Kumhars want to stop making pots and open a grocery shop. Using the concept of hereditary occupation, explain why this move faces resistance from both Brahmins and Chamars.
questions.a: Hereditary occupation means each caste has a monopoly on its traditional work and a duty to perform it. If Kumhars leave pottery, Brahmins lose their ritual service providers, and Chamars lose a buffer caste that maintains the hierarchy. Resistance comes because the system relies on *complementary, non-competing* roles; one caste’s exit threatens the whole structure. A wrong answer focusing only on “economic competition” ignores the ritual-service obligation that binds castes together.

questions.q: Compare how hierarchy operates in the caste system versus in a class system. Identify two similarities and two differences, referencing purity-pollution and economic capital.
questions.a: Similarities: both rank groups unequally and affect life chances. Differences: (1) Caste hierarchy is ritual (purity-pollution) and ascribed at birth; class hierarchy is economic (capital) and potentially achievable. (2) Caste hierarchy is closed (no mobility); class hierarchy is relatively open. A wrong answer that says “both are based on money” conflates ritual status with economic class and misses the unique *ritual* foundation of caste hierarchy.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: “Hereditary occupation is the economic base of caste; without it, the caste system would collapse.” Use evidence from the NCERT text about colonialism and modern industry.
questions.a: The statement is partially true but incomplete. Colonialism and modern industry *did* create jobs with no caste rules, yet caste persisted through endogamy and hierarchy. The NCERT notes recruitment in mills remained caste-based, and endogamy stayed strong. So hereditary occupation is *one* pillar; the system survives even when that pillar weakens because the other two (endogamy, hierarchy) compensate. A wrong answer that agrees wholly ignores the resilience shown in the text.

questions.q: Create a short case study (150 words) of a fictional village where a lower-caste family attempts to educate their daughter for a government job. Show how all three pillars — hierarchy, hereditary occupation, and endogamy — create barriers at each step.
questions.a: A good case study will show: (1) Hierarchy — teachers/school officials discriminate (purity-pollution), denying her equal attention. (2) Hereditary occupation — village elders pressure her to do traditional work, saying “your caste’s duty is X.” (3) Endogamy — when she succeeds, marriage proposals dry up because higher castes won’t marry “up” and her own caste sees her as “too modern.” A poor case study treats barriers as isolated incidents rather than interconnected systemic forces.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Caste as a system of ______ is a hereditary, endogamous, and hierarchical social structure where membership is fixed by birth, occupations are traditionally inherited, and social ranking is justified by concepts of ritual purity and pollution, creating a closed system of unequal life chances.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are at a village wedding where the bride and groom are from the same caste, the priest chants Sanskrit verses, and the food is cooked only by a ______ caste — why does this scene feel “normal” to many Indians?
What is Caste as a system of stratification? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Caste as a system of stratification is a hereditary, endogamous, and hierarchical social structure where membership is fixed by birth, occupations are traditionally inherited, and social ranking is justified by concepts of ritual purity and pollution, creating a closed system of unequal life chances.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Caste as a system of stratification?
questions.a: Students often think “caste is just like class but older” — they equate hierarchy with economic inequality and assume hereditary occupation is merely a division of labour.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how hierarchy, hereditary occupation, and endogamy interlock to reproduce caste inequality, and can analyze a real-world scenario (e.g., marriage patterns, occupational segregation) to identify which caste feature is operating and why it persists despite legal abolition.
